How big is the Atacama Desert? The Atacama Desert covers an area of 105,000 km2, bordering Peru to the north and the Chilean Matorral ecoregion to the south. Why is the Atacama Desert so dry? Nestled between two mountain chains, the Andes and the Chilean Coast Range, this desert is essentially blocked off from moisture. From the east, the Andes block the westward-moving humidity coming from the Amazon, and the cold Humboldt Current to the west chills the air above the Pacific, making it nearly impossible for clouds to rise and release rain. These unique conditions leave parts of the Atacama Desert with virtually no precipitation year-round. The average annual rainfall there is around 15mm – for contrast, the Sahara averages about 75mm, while London racks up 600mm annually. And in certain regions of the Atacama, even the modest 15mm can seem like a lot. passages.text: Stretching along an over 1,000km-long strip of land in northern Chile, west of the Andes, is the Atacama Desert – the driest non-polar desert in the world. - The world’s largest desert is enormous and there’s hardly any rain – but it’s not hot. Here’s why - What’s the hottest place on Earth? And where's the biggest desert? Iconic landscapes such as the Valley of the Moon or the Valley of Death (also called Mars Valley), both near the town of San Pedro de Atacama, Chile, make this desert one of the most otherworldly places on the planet. The high altitude, dry air and almost total absence of light pollution make the Atacama Desert one of the world’s premier sites for astronomical observation and home to powerful radio telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA). The soil composition and nearly total absence of microbial life have also made parts of this desert a perfect testing ground for Mars mission instruments. But it's not all arid and barren – when the conditions are just right, the Atacama Desert can surprise you with an array of colours fit for a garden. How big is the Atacama Desert? Aridity in Atacama Desert predates the rise of the Central Andes, yet hyper-aridity is generally thought to have resulted from the rise of the Andes.[30] As such it is hypothesised it had climatic conditions akin to the Namib Desert prior to the rise of the mountains.[30] The Atacama is so arid that many mountains higher than 6,000 m (20,000 ft) are completely free of glaciers. Only the highest peaks (such as Ojos del Salado, Monte Pissis, and – debatably[31][32][33][34][35] – Llullaillaco) have some permanent snow coverage. The southern part of the desert, between 25° and 27°S, may have been glacier-free throughout the Quaternary (including during glaciations), though permafrost extends down to an altitude of 4,400 m (14,400 ft) and is continuous above 5,600 m (18,400 ft). Studies by a group of British scientists have suggested that some river beds have been dry for 120,000 years.[36] However, some locations in the Atacama receive a marine fog known locally as the camanchaca, providing sufficient moisture for hypolithic algae, lichens, and even some cacti—the genus Copiapoa is notable among these. passages.text: Why Does the Atacama Desert Not Get Rain? The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth, with some areas receiving almost no rainfall for centuries. But why doesn’t it rain in the Atacama? The answer lies in a mix of geographical, climatic, and atmospheric factors. From powerful wind patterns to ocean currents that block moisture, several forces make this desert an extreme and fascinating environment. In this article by thedailyECO, we’ll explore the science behind the Atacama’s dryness and how life survives in such an inhospitable place. What is the Atacama Desert? Along South America's west coast, in Chile, stretches the Atacama Desert, a 1,600-kilometer (994-mile) expanse that is Earth's driest non-polar desert. Covering 105,000 square kilometers (40,541 square miles) this region sits between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes mountains. Its extreme aridity means some areas might wait 10, 40, or even more years for a mere millimeter of rainfall. Despite these harsh conditions, life finds ways to thrive here. When rare rainfall occurs, the desert awakens during the "desierto florido" (flowering desert), as dormant seeds burst into colorful blooms across the land. Xeropreservation of functionalized lipid biomarkers in hyperarid soils in the Atacama Desert The extreme dryness has also allowed unusual chemical deposits to accumulate on the surface. Natural perchlorate, for example, is found in Atacama soils in concentrations far higher than anywhere else on Earth. Isotope data support the idea that this perchlorate was deposited from the atmosphere over millions of years and simply never washed away, because there has been so little rain to dissolve it.7Environmental Research. Perchlorate contamination in Chile: Legacy, challenges, and potential solutions When It Does Rain The Atacama is not absolutely rainless everywhere and always. Rare but sometimes intense rainfall does occur, almost exclusively tied to El Niño events. During an El Niño, the warming of eastern Pacific waters disrupts the normal atmospheric patterns that keep the desert dry. The 1982–83 El Niño, estimated at the time as the most severe of the century, pushed rain southward along the Peruvian coast and into northern Chile, with sporadic showers continuing for months. passages.text: The Atacama Desert is dry because it sits at the intersection of three powerful drying mechanisms that reinforce one another: a semi-permanent high-pressure system that pushes sinking air over the region, the cold Humboldt Current running along the coast that chills moisture out of the atmosphere before it can reach land, and the Andes Mountains rising sharply to the east, blocking humid air from the Amazon basin. Any one of these would create arid conditions. Together, they produce a place where some weather stations have never recorded measurable rainfall, and where parts of the landscape have been functionally rainless for millions of years. The Subtropical High-Pressure System The single biggest driver of Atacama aridity is its position beneath the southeastern Pacific subtropical anticyclone, a broad zone of high atmospheric pressure that sits over the ocean off South America’s western coast. Air within this system sinks from high altitude toward the surface, warming and drying as it descends. Because it is sinking, it resists being displaced by weather fronts that might carry moisture. Beneath the desert floor, groundwater systems hold water that fell as rain thousands or even millions of years ago. passages.text: Perhaps surprisingly, it’s not uncommon to see gatherings of South American fur seals and South American sea lions along the coast. The most diverse animal group in the Atacama is birds. Humboldt penguins live along the coast year-round, and inland salt flats are inhabited by Andean flamingos. Several species of hummingbirds and rufous-collared sparrow frequent the lomas seasonally to feed on insects, nectar, seeds and flowers. Are there any plants in the Atacama Desert? The Atacama has a surprisingly rich variety of flora – the most common species are herbs and flowers such as thyme, llareta and saltgrass, and where humidity allows it, trees like the tamarugo (endemic to the desert), the chañar, the pimiento tree and the algarrobo grow. But, when the conditions are just right, something astonishing occurs in the spring – a phenomenon known as ‘desert bloom’, when more than 200 types of flowers bloom in the Atacama, bathing the usually subdued desert in colour. For the desert to bloom, a very precise combination of rain and cold is needed. Between 15 and 30mm of rainfall, mainly between June and July, plus a buildup of enough cold hours – and the dormant seeds beneath the soil awaken.

And if you think that sounds dry, there is even evidence suggesting the desert may have received no significant rainfall from 1570 to 1971. How old is the Atacama Desert? Until recently, scientists dated the hyper-arid conditions in this desert back to Early or Mid-Miocene, approx. 10-20 million years ago. But recent studies have presented evidence that the area was already experiencing hyper-aridity shortly after global cooling – around 45 million years ago. “This makes it one of the longest continuously dry regions on Earth and forces us to reconsider how and when such extreme environments develop,” says Dr Benedikt Ritter-Prinz from the Institute for Geology & Mineralogy at the University of Cologne, Germany. Because of the desert's extreme aridity, only a few specially adapted mammal species live in the Atacama, such as Darwin's leaf-eared mouse. The less arid parts of the desert are inhabited by the South American gray fox and the viscacha (a relative of the chinchilla). Larger animals, such as guanacos and vicuñas, graze in areas where grass grows, mainly because it is seasonally irrigated by melted snow. Vicuñas need to remain near a steady water supply, while guanacos can roam into more arid areas and survive longer without fresh water. South American fur seals and South American sea lions often gather along the coast.
